stories.summary: Africa: United States Accused of Exploiting Migrant Suffering With Africa Deportations New Dawn U.S. Transferees arriving at the Robert International Airport in Monrovia (file photo). 8 October 2026 Radio France Internationale By RFI The United States is violating international law by deporting migrants to African countries where they have no ties, NGO Human Rights Watch said on Thursday, accusing Washington of using deportation to remote destinations as a deterrent to immigration. United States deportation policy has expanded sharply since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, with his administration striking agreements with governments in Africa, Latin America and the Pacific to receive foreign nationals who cannot legally be returned to their own countries. More than 500 people have since been deported from the US to African countries other than their own, according to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) data cited by Human Rights Watch . stories.title: Mozambique: Cashew Nuts Smuggling Causes 457 Million Meticais Loss
stories.summary: Mozambique: Cashew Nuts Smuggling Causes 457 Million Meticais Loss 8 October 2026 Agencia de Informacao de Mocambique (Maputo) By Zelio Tembe Maputo — Mozambican government has recorded, over the last three years, the loss of 457 million meticais (about 7.2 million US dollars at the current exchange rate) as a result of cashew nuts smuggling. According to Roberto Albino, Minister of Agriculture, speaking at the first session of the Cashew Committee, about 35,000 tonnes of cashew nuts were smuggled during the period. In order to reverse the situation, the minister called for tougher actions against those involved in the illegal trade of this product. "I believe that if we want to end smuggling, we have to stop treating smugglers merely as administrative offenders. We have to criminalize it", he said. The losses, the minister said, went beyond foregone revenue, as the diversion of cashew nuts from formal channels also prevents the country from benefiting from foreign-exchange earnings generated by exports.

stories.summary: Nigeria: NAF Explains Confusion Over 25, 32 Crash Victims 8 October 2026 Vanguard (Lagos) By Kingsley Omonobi The Nigerian Air Force (NAF) has explained the discrepancy in the reported number of victims of the ATR 42 aircraft crash at Igbokoda, Ondo State, saying a misunderstanding of civil and military aviation terminology led to the initial figure of 32 persons being reported. Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, who provided the clarification, said the confusion arose from the different ways civil aviation air traffic controllers and the military use the term "souls on board." Ejodame explained that while civil aviation terminology could describe the number as "25 souls on board, inclusive of seven crew," military usage counts the seven crew members within the total figure of 25, rather than adding them to it. He said: "For air traffic controllers, when they normally communicate '25 souls on board inclusive of seven crew', it is minus the seven. stories.title: Rwanda: Trade to Energy - What Is Driving Stronger Rwanda-Kenya Ties?
stories.summary: Rwanda: Trade to Energy - What Is Driving Stronger Rwanda-Kenya Ties? 8 October 2026 The New Times (Kigali) analysis By Charles Nyandwi Rwanda and Kenya have signed 11 new MOUs (memoranda of understanding) but the latest agreements are only one part of a bilateral relationship being increasingly driven by trade, transport and logistics, energy, investment, tourism and the movement of people. The agreements were concluded during the 10th Session of the Kenya-Rwanda Joint Permanent Commission for Cooperation (JPCC), held in Nairobi from October 5-6. The meeting reviewed progress since the previous session in Kigali in 2023 and identified areas where cooperation should be accelerated. The new instruments cover mutual legal assistance in criminal matters and the transfer of sentenced persons, as well as political consultations, immigration, housing and urban development, diaspora management, water resources and irrigation, local governance, cooperation between Rwanda Investigation Bureau and Kenya National Police Service, culture and heritage, and conservation. Beyond the agreements, however, the expanding relationship is increasingly visible in the flow of goods, investments, petroleum products, tourists, professionals and cargo between the two countries.

Une décision saluée par l’Association nationale des chrétiens contre la torture (Acat) : « Le mandat de Rapporteur spécial montre que la situation du Burundi n'est pas oubliée sur la scène internationale. » Publié le : 08/10/2026 - 10:37 2 min Temps de lecture [Image d'archives] Le rapporteur spécial des Nations unies, Fortuné Gaëtan Zongo, présentant son premier rapport sur la situation des droits de l'homme au Burundi lors d'une session du 51e Conseil des droits de l'homme des Nations unies à Genève, le 23 septembre 2022. AFP - FABRICE COFFRINI Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Au Burundi , la société civile exprime son soulagement ce mercredi après l’adoption la veille mardi à Genève, par le Conseil des droits de l’homme de l’ONU, d’une résolution sur le pays. NCDs caused an estimated 2.33 billion cases and 4.70 million deaths. The leading causes of NCD deaths in 2023 were, Ischaemic heart disease - 801,000 deaths, stroke - 700,000, chronic kidney disease - 293,000, hypertensive heart disease - 246,000 and diabetes - 245,000. stories.title: ‘There’s always been a belittling of African women’: honouring history’s invisible heroines
stories.summary: As demand for it drove the transatlantic slave trade, sugar symbolises the sacrifice of people for goods. Photograph: Pamela Tulizo Congolese photographer Pamela Tulizo uses costume and vivid scenery to celebrate women’s strength and give a new perspective on slavery By Sarah Johnson P amela Tulizo’s latest series of photographs started with a question. “I asked myself, why are women in my community in particular, and African women in general, so strong?” says Tulizo, an artist and photographer from the Democratic Republic of the Congo . “Where does this strength come from?” Growing up in Goma in eastern DRC, Tulizo was informed and inspired by the women she was surrounded by, including her mother, her sisters, her mother’s friends and her neighbours. Years later, when she began to look into the role of women throughout African history, she says: “I realised that perhaps women have been forced to be strong since the dawn of time, forced by circumstance to build that resilience.” View image in fullscreen Women are placed at the centre of the series of 23 staged photographs Her research brought her to slavery, the “cruellest period in human history”, which is often just associated with the men who were forced across oceans to form workforces abroad. Women, she noticed, were largely invisible, their stories untold. With that in mind, Tulizo placed women at the centre of her series of 23 staged photographs called Mababu (“ancestors” in Swahili).

The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC. Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.

stories.title: Anthropic report: Is Russia using AI for disinformation in the Central African Republic and elsewhere across Africa?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NTaF The Claude app was allegedly misused by Russian agents Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic , Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence. A report titled " Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI ," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported. The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world. stories.title: Knox Chitiyo obituary
stories.summary: Knox Chitiyo left Zimbabwe in 2005 to live in the UK, where he was head of the Royal United Services Institute’s Africa programme View image in fullscreen Knox Chitiyo left Zimbabwe in 2005 to live in the UK, where he was head of the Royal United Services Institute’s Africa programme Obituary Knox Chitiyo obituary My friend and former colleague Knox Chitiyo, who has died aged 65 of bowel cancer, was a Zimbabwean academic and later an important voice in Britain on his homeland and its future. He was regularly consulted by diplomats, business people, journalists, academics and activists. From 1992 to 2003 he was a senior lecturer in war studies and military history at the University of Zimbabwe, where he co-founded the Centre for Defence Studies, serving as its deputy director. He also taught on the joint command and staff course at Zimbabwe’s National Army Staff College and at the Gweru Military Academy, helping shape the strategic thinking of a generation of officers. As intellectual space in Zimbabwe tightened under Robert Mugabe , Knox moved to the UK in 2005.

stories.title: Morocco's first female head of government: Symbol or real reform?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NfFo Mansouri has been nicknamed the "pasha's daughter" because she comes from a prominent Marrakesh family and her father was formerly a pasha or municipal governor Image: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP Advertisement After the announcement that Morocco would appoint its first female head of government – Marrakech mayor Fatima Zahra Mansouri – citizens interviewed by local television reporters were mostly enthusiastic. "It would be great if we had a female prime minister for a change. She'd lift our spirits a bit," one woman said. "Why don't we give women a chance? We've never had one [a female head of government] before," said another. "May God bless her and help her stay on a straight path." "Regardless of who takes on the role, it should be a change for the better in Morocco," a man added. Morocco's King Mohammed VI chose Fatima Zahra Mansouri to be the country's first female prime minister following September's parliamentary elections Image: Mosa'ab Elshamy/AP Photo/picture alliance But there were also naysayers. Some locals questioned how she would take part in official events where tradition and protocol dictate that only men attend. "People are saying that a nation cannot succeed if a woman is in charge, even if she's only half in charge," one man told a television reporter, referring to the fact that Morocco's King Mohammed VI has the final say in national politics.

stories.title: The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
stories.summary: Image source, Christian Parkinson/ BBC Image caption, Kgomotso Mathekga says a lack of male role models is fuelling violence against women in his neighbourhood By Christian Parkinson Reporting from Johannesburg Published 3 October 2026 "I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk." "I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her." Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa. The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township. "Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am." At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust. At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.

stories.title: John Iliffe obituary
stories.summary: John Iliffe’s work was regarded internationally as the model of what engaged research should be. Photograph: Nordin Ćatić/St John's College, Cambridge View image in fullscreen John Iliffe’s work was regarded internationally as the model of what engaged research should be. Photograph: Nordin Ćatić/St John's College, Cambridge Obituary John Iliffe obituary Pioneering historian who transformed the study of Africa by seeking out the testimonies of Africans When John Iliffe, who has died aged 87, wrote his book The African Poor: A History (1987), the continent was readily dismissed by many academics as a home of problems and poverty, with no intellectual depth. But Iliffe acknowledged no such limitations, and it came as no surprise that it won the African Studies Association’s best book prize, then known as the Herskovits prize. In Iliffe’s view, people who are excluded from production, productive resources and land in otherwise land-rich economies are not just statistics who merely suffer.

stories.title: Trump is disappearing refugees into the hands of torturers – and rewarding them handsomely | Tutu Alicante and Uzra Zeya
stories.summary: ‘Adam and everyone held at Hotel Bamy should be released and given the chance to have their asylum claims heard in a country capable of hearing them.’ Photograph: Monika Pronczuk/AP View image in fullscreen ‘Adam and everyone held at Hotel Bamy should be released and given the chance to have their asylum claims heard in a country capable of hearing them.’ Photograph: Monika Pronczuk/AP Trump is disappearing refugees into the hands of torturers – and rewarding them handsomely Tutu Alicante and Uzra Zeya Refugees from third countries are being sent to Equatorial Guinea, where they are often sent back to the very countries they fled F or nearly a year, the Hotel Bamy in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea , has been Adam’s prison. He is confined alone to a hotel room, under constant watch by the security officers and soldiers of a notoriously oppressive regime who control his movements. Not long ago, they barged into his room, handcuffed and beat him, and warned him not to tell anyone. There is no cell to point to, no charges or formal sentence, and nothing on paper to document his plight. Adam, 26, has chosen not to share his real name or even his country of origin out of fear for his safety.

stories.title: How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia
stories.summary: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Tigrayan forces have been patrolling the streets of Tigray's capital, Mekelle, this week By Lucy Fleming Â and Â BBC Africa Published 26 September 2026 Updated 2 October 2026 Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army. Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict. There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted. This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago. Why has fighting broken out now?

stories.title: Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin
stories.summary: The mural in Tahrir Square was designed by a volunteer youth group, Rasmet Basma, with the help of AI. Photograph: Rasmet Basma View image in fullscreen The mural in Tahrir Square was designed by a volunteer youth group, Rasmet Basma, with the help of AI. Photograph: Rasmet Basma Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric claims about pharaohs’ origins On the eve of the Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight. Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by a group of young volunteers, Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square. But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the 14th-century BCE pharaoh’s origins.

stories.title: Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
stories.summary: Image source, Reuters By Barbara Plett Usher Africa correspondent ,Â Reporting from Nairobi, Kangema & Meru Published 2 October 2026 Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya. The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people. The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics â by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up.
